summary: Lesotho is a landlocked mountain country completely surrounded by South Africa. Its entire territory lies above 1,000 meters in altitude, earning it the name "Kingdom in the Sky", and it became independent from Britain in 1966.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In 1833 Moshoeshoe I invited missionaries of the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society of France to establish a mission station at Morija, the first Christian base in Lesotho. The missionaries translated the Bible into Sesotho and founded schools and a printing press, so Protestantism (today the Evangelical Church of Lesotho) has had a profound influence among the Basotho and has shaped the country's literate and political elite.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1862 missionaries of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate arrived and founded a mission station at Roma, which later developed into the forerunner of the National University of Lesotho. Catholicism expanded its influence through schools, hospitals and rural services, grew rapidly in the 20th century, and is today the single largest denomination in Lesotho, though it and Protestantism were at times rival camps in politics.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: These include Anglicanism, Pentecostalism introduced in the 20th century, and African independent churches such as Zionist churches. Zionist and similar churches blend elements of healing, ancestral spirits and Christianity, and are very popular among miners and rural residents in Lesotho and South Africa.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Lesotho has a strongly religious atmosphere, and few people explicitly state that they have no religion, mainly educated young people in cities; most people, even if they seldom go to church, take part in church and traditional rituals.

religion.background: The traditional belief of the Basotho centers on the worship of ancestral spirits (balimo). In the 1820s, during the turmoil of the "Mfecane" wars in southern Africa, Moshoeshoe I gathered various clans on Thaba Bosiu mountain and founded the Basotho kingdom. In 1833 he invited Protestant missionaries of the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society of France into the country, hoping to use European knowledge and diplomacy to resist the Boers and other forces; in 1862 the Catholic Oblates of Mary Immaculate also came to Lesotho. In 1868 Lesotho became a British protectorate (Basutoland), and the churches became the main providers of schools and medical care. After independence in 1966 Christianity became the faith of the great majority, but ancestor worship and traditional rituals still coexist with Christianity.

language.official: Sesotho and English are the official languages.

ranking.name: Sesotho
ranking.description: Lesotho is a rare single-nation state in Africa, with the great majority of its population being Basotho, and when Moshoeshoe I founded the state he united the various clans under the Sesotho language. In the 19th century missionaries devised a writing system for it and published the Bible and literary works. After independence, Sesotho and English became joint official languages, and Sesotho is widely used in schools, government and broadcasting.

ranking.name: Zulu
ranking.description: Zulu speakers live mainly along Lesotho's eastern border, near South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province. During the Mfecane wars and the expansion of the Zulu kingdom in the 19th century, some Nguni people moved into this area and lived mixed with the Basotho.

ranking.name: Xhosa
ranking.description: Xhosa speakers are mainly found in southern Lesotho, in the Quthing area bordering South Africa's Eastern Cape province. They are descendants of Nguni groups who moved in during the 19th century, and today most of them also use Sesotho.

language.history: Sesotho belongs to the Sotho-Tswana group of the Bantu language family and is the language of the Basotho. In the 1830s French missionaries devised a writing system for Sesotho using the Latin alphabet, and a complete Sesotho Bible was published in the late 19th century; the printing press at Morija also published works by writers such as Thomas Mofolo, giving Sesotho one of the earliest indigenous literary traditions in Africa. After Lesotho became a British protectorate in 1868, English became the administrative language. After independence in 1966, Sesotho and English became joint official languages, and because the national ethnic composition is homogeneous, Sesotho is the mother tongue of the great majority.

ranking.name: Papa (maize porridge)
ranking.description: A stiff porridge ball cooked from white maize meal and eaten with vegetable stews or meat, it is the most basic staple food of Lesotho. It has a solid texture and a mild taste, and is mainly eaten with stews, vegetables or sour milk.
ranking.history: Maize is native to the Americas and was introduced to Lesotho in the 19th century via European settlers and missionaries from South Africa, gradually replacing traditional sorghum as the staple. In the late 19th century large numbers of Basotho men went to work in South African diamond and gold mines, and maize meal also became widespread through the mines' ration system. Today papa is eaten at almost every meal, cooked in a large pot and shared by the whole family.

ranking.name: Moroho (wild greens)
ranking.description: Wild or cultivated leafy greens (such as spinach, beet leaves and wild amaranth) are cooked with onion and tomato and eaten with papa.
ranking.history: Moroho is the Basotho general term for vegetable side dishes, traditionally made by women from wild plants gathered in the fields. Because Lesotho's mountains are cold and meat is expensive, moroho is the main source of nutrition on the everyday table. In the dry season and winter, people also dry vegetables to preserve them to get through the season of scarcity.

ranking.name: Lebese (sour milk)
ranking.description: Milk is allowed to ferment naturally in a gourd or container into thick, sour-tasting soured milk, often eaten with papa. It is thick, tangy, and rich in protein.
ranking.history: Since ancient times the Basotho have relied on herding cattle as an important livelihood, and cattle represent wealth and bride price (bohali). Fermented milk is a way of preserving milk, particularly important in the mountains where there are no refrigerators. Traditionally, in making lebese, men milk the cattle while women ferment and distribute it, and it remains an important source of protein for rural families.

ranking.name: Chakalaka
ranking.description: A spicy vegetable relish stir-cooked from onion, tomato, chili, baked beans and carrot, served as a side dish with papa or grilled meat.
ranking.history: Chakalaka is generally thought to have originated in the gold-mining areas of Johannesburg, South Africa, in the 20th century, where miners from Mozambique and other neighboring countries cooked a spicy side dish from canned food and chili, eaten with maize porridge. Because large numbers of Basotho men worked in South African mines, the dish was brought to Lesotho and became a common side dish at barbecues and gatherings.

ranking.name: Joala (sorghum beer)
ranking.description: A cloudy, slightly sour, low-alcohol traditional beer brewed from sprouted sorghum. With low alcohol content and a slightly sour taste with a grain aroma, it is often shared at festivals and ceremonies.
ranking.history: Sorghum was Lesotho's main grain before maize arrived, and joala brewed from sorghum has important social and ritual significance in Basotho society. At weddings, initiation rites, offerings to ancestors and village cooperative labor (letsema), sorghum beer must be prepared to host everyone. During the colonial period the authorities restricted the sale of traditional alcohol, but joala has continued in the countryside to this day.
